stories.title: The LED Chess Computer
stories.description: Ajay recalls his first 'state of the art' electronic purchase in protectionist India—a tiny chess computer with blinking LEDs, brought by a neighbor from Singapore. He contrasts this with the modern world where black markets for chips have returned.

stories.title: Shanghai Chip Black Market
stories.description: Ajay notes that despite global trade, we are back to a black market for chips (like Nvidia A100s) in places like Shanghai and Kazakhstan, reminiscent of pre-1991 India where you had to 'nudge nudge wink wink' to get banned goods.

stories.title: NSE Risk Management System
stories.description: In the early 90s, NSE wanted a real-time risk management system. They visited Chicago but found the US tech obsolete. Susan Thomas and Ashish Chauhan proposed building a 'Beowulf cluster' of cheap Intel CPUs to do parallel computing. It worked (Project 'Prism') and is still the basis of NSE's system. This illustrates that 'parallel computing' can overcome lack of high-end hardware.

stories.title: The Three-Legged Stool
stories.description: The US strategy against China has three legs: Industrial Policy (subsidies like CHIPS Act), Tariffs, and Export Controls (blocking chips/IP).

core_ideas.description: We have moved from the 'Second Globalization' (unconditional access) to the 'Third Globalization' (access conditional on good behavior/alignment). The core of the world economy has decided that access is no longer a free lunch.
The US is using its central position in the global economy (IP, finance, software) to choke off adversaries, using tools like the FDPR to control products made outside the US if they use US tech.
It's not just trade; it's about military capacity (Taiwan, Ukraine). The West realized that funding Russia/China via trade was undermining their own security.

core_ideas.item: Export Controls as a Delay Tactic
core_ideas.description: You can't stop a country from building a nuclear bomb (fixed target) forever, but you can slow them down in an 'arms race' (like drones) where being 2 months ahead matters.
Sanctions might force China to dominate legacy chips (which they are doing), hurting Western firms. It also encourages indigenous innovation (though difficult).
As shown by the NSE story, you can often achieve high-end compute by stringing together many low-end chips, making sanctions less effective for some tasks (like nuclear simulations).
